Some of Nvidia Corp.’s biggest customers have been told that the prices of servers containing its artificial intelligence chips are going up more than 15% in many cases with memory chip costs soaring.

The price hikes will go into effect on systems shipped early next year and will impact systems including those with the flagship Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell chips, according to people familiar with the process, who asked to not to be identified commenting on communications that haven’t yet been made public. highlights:
## The numerator: what accelerator time costs

| Instance or plan | Rate | Source (observed 22 Aug 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lambda, 8× NVIDIA H100 SXM 80 GB | $3.99 per GPU per hour | Lambda GPU cloud |
| Lambda, 1× NVIDIA H100 SXM 80 GB | $4.29 per GPU per hour | Lambda GPU cloud |
| Lambda, 8× NVIDIA A100 SXM 80 GB | $2.79 per GPU per hour | Lambda GPU cloud |
| Lambda, 8× NVIDIA B200 SXM6 180 GB | $6.69 per GPU per hour | Lambda GPU cloud |
| AWS Capacity Blocks, `p5.48xlarge` (8× H100), US East (N. Virginia) | $41.528 per hour per instance, $5.191 per accelerator | EC2 Capacity Blocks pricing |
| AWS Capacity Blocks, `p5.4xlarge` (1× H100), US East (N. Virginia) | $5.191 per hour | EC2 Capacity Blocks pricing |
| AWS Capacity Blocks, `p6-b200.48xlarge` (8× B200), US East (Ohio) | $98.84 per hour per instance, $12.355 per accelerator | EC2 Capacity Blocks pricing |

Two observations about this table that matter more than the individual figures.

The single-GPU rate is higher per GPU than the eight-GPU rate: $4.29 against $3.99 for H100 SXM (Lambda GPU cloud, observed 22 August 2026). Small deployments pay a premium per unit of capacity, which works against the case for a modest self-hosted footprint.

...

## Reserved against on-demand capacity

Once you accept that you are buying time, the question becomes how far ahead you buy it. The published spread is wide.

| Purchasing mode | Published terms | Source (observed 22 Aug 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Google Cloud Spot VMs | Up to 91% below on-demand rates for GPUs, TPUs and general machine types; Compute Engine can preempt at any time | Compute Engine pricing |
| Google Cloud committed use discounts | Up to 70% below on-demand for memory-optimized types with a term commitment | Compute Engine pricing |
| AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks | Reservation fee charged up front at the time the reservation is scheduled, plus an operating system fee | EC2 Capacity Blocks pricing |
| Vertex AI Provisioned Throughput, 1 week commit | $7.14 per GSU per hour, global endpoints | Vertex AI pricing |
| Vertex AI Provisioned Throughput, 1 month commit | $3.698630137 per GSU per hour, global endpoints | Vertex AI pricing |
| Vertex AI Provisioned Throughput, 1 year commit | $2.739726027 per GSU per hour, global endpoints | Vertex AI pricing |

The Vertex AI rows show the shape of the trade with a vendor’s own numbers: the hourly rate falls as the commitment lengthens, and the gap is the price of keeping your options open. Google also notes on its Compute Engine pricing page that Spot prices are variable and can change up to once a day, and that Spot instances are recommended only for fault-tolerant workloads. Spot capacity is therefore usable for batch inference and evaluation runs, and not for anything with a latency SLO attached to a user.

AWS adds a caution worth quoting for anyone building a multi-quarter model: its Capacity Blocks pricing page states that reservation prices are updated regularly based on trends in supply and demand, that the current prices were scheduled to be updated next in October 2026, and that a block is charged at the prevailing rate at the time of purchase. Accelerator capacity is priced like a scarce commodity because it is one.

highlights:
# El mercado de GPU-cloud ya tiene carta de menú y precios publicados. | Ervin Muñoz Ortiz · LinkedIn · 2026-08-22T00:00:00+00:00

**Ervin Muñoz Ortiz**: Fundador @ Escala+ | Marketing + IA + Automatización para PyMEs en México · CRM, Agentes IA, Ads Meta/Google, Contenido a escala.

---

El mercado de GPU-cloud ya tiene carta de menú y precios publicados.

CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda, Crusoe y Groq operan con modelos distintos: dos públicos (CoreWeave $2.575M ingresos Q2, backlog $104M; Nebius $582M, 49.7% EBITDA ajustado), tres privados con acuerdos de miles de millones con Microsoft, Oracle y OpenAI. Los precios on-demand por GPU-hora hoy: H100 $3.90–6.16, H200 $4.29–6.16, B200 $6.69–8.60, B300 solo en Nebius a $7.85. Crusoe ofrece MI300X (AMD) en carta; Lambda no tiene spot; Nebius subasta capacidad a >$40M/MW en corto plazo.

Lectura ejecutiva:
· La brecha entre list price y precio real de contrato supera el 10–15% según SemiAnalysis; negocie sobre volumen anual, no sobre tarifa web.
· Si su carga es inferencia estable, reserve capacidad anual (base ~$12M/MW en Nebius); si es esporádica, use preemptible/spot a ~45% de descuento.
· La aparición de AMD MI300X en Crusoe rompe el monopolio NVIDIA en carta pública; evalúelo para workloads de inferencia donde el ratio precio/rendimiento cierre.

En la mesa del C-level: la decisión ya no es "qué GPU" sino "qué proveedor y modelo contractual" para cada carga de trabajo.

results.title: Nvidia to Implement Over 15% Price Hikes on AI Servers | Borsaya.com
highlights:
# Nvidia to Implement Over 15% Price Hikes on AI Servers

Chipmaker Nvidia has reportedly informed some of its largest customers that prices for servers containing its AI chips will rise by more than 15%. According to Bloomberg News, these increases are driven by soaring memory chip costs and will affect systems shipped in early 2026.

Borsaya Newsroom

August 22, 2026 at 08:26 PM

Nvidia, a leading player in the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market, has notified some of its major customers about price increases exceeding 15% for servers equipped with its AI chips. According to information reported by Bloomberg News, these price hikes are primarily driven by significant rises in the cost of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and GDDR7 memory modules. This decision by the company is expected to further intensify cost pressures in the industry amidst the continuously growing demand for global AI infrastructure.

Nvidia's price increases will apply to systems shipped in early 2026. This will affect various configurations, including those built around the company's flagship Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell chips. The exact magnitude of the price adjustments will vary depending on the chip generation and memory configuration ordered. While server-grade AI accelerators like the H200 and B200 are expected to see increases of up to 15%, wholesale prices for consumer graphics cards in the retail market have also reportedly seen bumps of 5% to 10%.

This development has been communicated to customers by companies that contract to build servers for major data center operators such as Microsoft, Alphabet's Google, and Oracle. Memory chip manufacturers Samsung Electronics, SK Hynex, and Micron Technology have gained unprecedented leverage due to the surging demand for AI infrastructure. These three companies account for a significant portion of global DRAM production, and the effectiveness of AI accelerator processors depends heavily on the amount of DRAM they are paired with.

results.title: Loose, Not Flooded
highlights:
GPU rentals dipped 5% this week. The reason isn't new H100 supply.

Bargo · 2026-08-22

GPU rental prices eased week over week on Aug 22, but the tape does not show a new H100 supply flood. The Compute Tightness Index fell to 47.1 Balanced from 54.8 a week earlier, still firmer than a month ago, while GPU rental prices split by generation. H100 and H200 softened, B200 on-demand rose 3.2%. For NVDA, that is bifurcated pricing power. For startups, it is cheaper to rent H100s this week, less reason to rush to buy.

## What the tape shows

The blended Compute Tightness Index (CTI, 0 to 100, higher is tighter) printed 47.1 on Aug 22, regime Balanced. That is down 7.7 points week over week from 54.8 on Aug 15, but up 2.4 points from about 44.7 on Jul 9. The 30-day change is essentially flat at +0.4 points, so this week is a give-back inside a July-to-August climb, not a new downtrend.

Per-GPU on Aug 22:

| GPU | On-demand avg | Spot avg | Spot discount vs on-demand | Listings | CTI | Regime |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | $3.86 | $1.75 | 55% | 158 | 40.0 | Loose |
| H200 | $4.32 | $2.97 | 31% | 71 | 59.2 | Balanced |
| B200 | $7.05 | $3.82 | 46% | 43 | 53.2 | Balanced |

Week over week (Aug 22 vs Aug 15):

| GPU | On-demand WoW | Spot WoW | Listings change | Unavailable change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | -1.0% | -4.4% | +6 (+3.9%) | 36 vs 118 (-69%) |
| H200 | -2.3% | -13.2% | -3 | 19 vs 54 (-65%) |
| B200 | +3.2% | +0.5% | +3 | 42 vs 88 (-52%) |

A simple three-GPU spot average was $2.85 vs $3.02 a week ago (-5.6%). On-demand averaged $5.08 vs $5.05 (+0.5%). Your $2.59 / -9.4% basket is directionally consistent but larger than this three-GPU cut, likely a different weighting.

...

## Supply vs demand: why it loosened

Not a H100 supply flood. H100 listings rose only 6 week over week, H200 listings fell. The 30-day CTI delta is flat for H100 (-0.1) and H200 (+0.2), firmer for B200 (+1.8). No surge in new supply across the board.

Availability normalized. The biggest WoW move was unavailable counts collapsing across all three GPUs, more capacity showing as available while listings barely moved. That reads as loosening, but the Aug 21 to Aug 22 drop was unusually sharp (H100 unavailable 151 to 36 in one day), so watch for a snap-back next week before calling it structural.

Demand softened short term, still strong medium term. Token Demand Index on this slice was 66.3T tokens per week on Aug 21 vs 70.2T on Aug 14 (-5.5% WoW), but vs 42.8T on Jul 13 (+54.8% MoM). Effective price per 1M tokens was $1.13 vs $1.16 WoW (-2.8%) and vs $2.31 a month ago (-51%). Inference pricing over about 30 days fell broadly, OpenAI -25.5%, Claude -40%, Google -12.2%, while open-source rose 4.2%. Falling token prices with rising volume is the classic Jevons pattern, price down, volume up, not demand collapse.

...

## What it means for NVDA pricing power

Bifurcated. B200 on-demand +3.2% WoW and spot +0.5% with CTI 53.2 Balanced shows frontier pricing power intact. H100 at CTI 40.0 Loose and 55% spot discount, and H200 spot -13.2%, show prior-generation discounting. That is consistent with a Balanced overall market, not Tight, where buyers can wait for H100 deals but still pay up for B200.

For context on how hyperscaler commitments frame NVDA

...

## What it means for AI startup CapEx

Cheaper H100 at $1.75 spot and H200 at $2.97 spot directly lowers near-term inference and training burn, so renting looks more attractive than buying this week. That defers CapEx urgency for startups that can stay on rented capacity.

It does not change the contracted buildout. The rental move is spot, the buildout is contracted. Startups renting from neoclouds benefit from lower prices now, but neoclouds themselves live on continuous issuance, so a sustained rental decline would pressure their utilization before it helps renters. Near term, rent vs build tilts to rent. Medium term, the decision still hinges on whether token volume re-accelerates after this -5.5% WoW dip.

As of August 22, 2026, an H100 rents for $2.69/hr on RunPod's Community Cloud, $3.29 on its Secure Cloud, $3.99 on Lambda, and $6.16 on CoreWeave on demand, all read from the vendors' pages the day this was written. Then spot inverts the whole table: CoreWeave's 8x H100 node drops from $49.24/hr to $19.71 on spot, which is $2.46 per GPU, cheaper than anyone's on-demand rate. The companies are as unalike as the prices: CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 and reported $5.13 billion in 2025 revenue, Lambda is reportedly on an IPO track for late 2026, and RunPod raised $100 million at a $1 billion valuation in June after turning down buyouts.

...

One trap before the details: normalize everything to price per GPU-hour. CoreWeave lists $49.24 for an HGX H100, which is an 8-GPU node ($6.16 per GPU, a figure its own table confirms in the single-GPU column), and its GB200 NVL72 instance at $42.00 is 4 GPUs ($10.50 each). Lambda and RunPod list per-GPU prices directly. Comparing a node price to a GPU price is the classic way this shopping trip goes wrong.

## CoreWeave

CoreWeave North America pricing table showing per-instance on-demand, spot, and single-GPU hourly prices: HGX H100 at $49.24 on demand, $19.71 spot, and $6.16 per GPU, HGX B200 at $68.80, GB200 NVL72 at $42.00, and A100 rows below

CoreWeave is the incumbent challenger that grew up: it priced its IPO at $40 a share on March 28, 2025, raising about $1.5 billion at a roughly $23 billion initial valuation, and reported $5.13 billion in 2025 revenue, up 168% year over year. Its attempted $9 billion all-stock acquisition of data center operator Core Scientific died on October 30, 2025 when Core Scientific's shareholders voted it down, so the land-grab continues by contract instead of merger.

The platform is Kubernetes-native: you get managed clusters and node pools rather than a simple VM picker, which is exactly right for fleets and exactly wrong for a weekend fine-tune. On-demand North America prices per 8-GPU instance: HGX H100 $49.24/hr, HGX H200 $50.44, HGX B200 $68.80, A100 $21.60, with GB300 and B300 behind contact-sales walls. The interesting column is spot: the HGX H100 falls to $19.71/hr ($2.46 per GPU) and the B200 to $34.11 ($4.26 per GPU), undercutting every on-demand price in this post if your training job checkpoints well enough to tolerate preemption.

Lambda instances pricing table on the 8x tab showing per-GPU hourly prices: B200 SXM6 at $6.69, H100 SXM at $3.99, A100 SXM 80GB at $2.79, A100 SXM 40GB at $1.99, and Tesla V100 at $0.79, with a sales tax footnote

Lambda sells the simplest mental model of the three: pick an instance, get a price per GPU-hour, plus applicable sales tax. On-demand 8x instances run $3.99 per H100 SXM, $2.79 per A100 80GB, $1.99 per A100 40GB, $6.69 per B200 SXM6, and a nostalgic $0.79 per V100. results.title: Nvidia Announces Over 15% Price Hikes on AI Products | KuCoin
highlights:
Release Time: 2026/08/22 19:22:43

Nvidia announced over 15% price hikes on AI products, including server GPUs like the H200 and B200, with early 2026 increases reaching 15%. Consumer cards rose 5-10% at wholesale, while retail prices for RTX 50-series models jumped up to 39% between June and August 2026. The RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPU rose 110% to $16,000. Analysts say enterprise costs could climb 20-30% when including full system impacts. This crypto price news highlights rising demand for HBM and GDDR7 modules. On-chain news shows continued pressure in the AI hardware market.

Nvidia has informed its customers and supply chain partners of price increases exceeding 15% on AI-related GPU products, adding fresh cost pressure to an industry already grappling with soaring demand for compute infrastructure.

The increases affect both server-grade AI accelerators and consumer graphics cards, with enterprise costs potentially climbing even higher once downstream markups are factored in.

## What’s driving the price hikes

The root cause is something called high-bandwidth memory, or HBM. Demand for HBM has exploded alongside the AI buildout, and suppliers have responded by raising prices.

GDDR7 memory modules have reportedly tripled in cost compared to prior generations.

Nvidia issued notifications to its add-in board partners in both May and July 2026, covering GPU kits that include the GPU die itself plus the VRAM. The affected lineup spans the latest Blackwell-generation GDDR7 products as well as older GDDR6-based models.

Server GPUs like the H200 and B200 have seen price increases of up to 15% in early 2026. Consumer cards have experienced more modest bumps of 5-10% at the wholesale level.

results.title: GPU Neoclouds Ranked for 2026: CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda…
highlights:
Key takeaways

- CoreWeave is the only Platinum-rated GPU cloud in SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX 2.0 and lists H100, H200, and B200 at premium rates.
- Nebius is the only provider in this group publishing on-demand pricing for the B300 GPU.
- Lambda publishes the lowest on-demand B200 rate at $6.69 per GPU-hour but offers no spot tier.
- Crusoe is the only provider in this group with AMD MI300X and MI355X on its public rate card.
- Groq became an NVIDIA Cloud Partner after licensing its LPU architecture to NVIDIA in December 2025, and plans to add NVIDIA GPU capacity.

Five companies now compete under the "neocloud" label, each with a distinct business model and pricing structure. CoreWeave and Nebius are public companies filing with the SEC; Lambda and Crusoe are private and heading toward IPOs; Groq relaunched as a pure inference-cloud business after licensing its LPU chip technology to NVIDIA in December 2025. A new comparison published by Marktechpost ranks all five on published pricing, deployed and contracted power, hardware roadmap, contract terms, and independent SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX 2.0 quality ratings.

## What happened

| Provider | Key fact |
| --- | --- |
| CoreWeave | Only Platinum rating in SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX 2.0; premium list pricing on H100, H200, B200 |
| Nebius | Only provider with published on-demand B300 pricing; files as a foreign private issuer (Form 6-K) |
| Lambda | Lowest published on-demand B200 rate: $6.69 per GPU-hour; no spot tier available |
| Crusoe | Only provider with AMD MI300X and MI355X on its public rate card |
| Groq | Licensed LPU architecture to NVIDIA (December 2025); now an NVIDIA Cloud Partner adding GPU capacity alongside LPU inference |

The comparison, published by Marktechpost on 21 August 2026, evaluates each provider on five dimensions: published pricing, deployed and contracted power capacity, hardware roadmap, contract structure, and third-party quality scores. The SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX 2.0 rating system is an independent benchmark that scores GPU cloud providers on cluster quality, networking, and reliability.

...

### CoreWeave: the premium tier

CoreWeave is a public company, reporting results on Form 10-Q each quarter. Its Platinum rating from SemiAnalysis is the highest in the ClusterMAX 2.0 system, and its list prices for H100, H200, and B200 reflect that positioning. Buyers pay more, but the independent quality score suggests they get a more consistent cluster.

### Nebius: the B300 early mover

Nebius, also public and filing Form 6-K as a foreign private issuer, is the only provider in this group with a published on-demand price for the B300 GPU. Being first to publish a rate card for next-generation hardware is a meaningful signal for teams planning workloads around NVIDIA’s newest silicon.

### Lambda: cheapest B200 on-demand

Lambda’s $6.69 per GPU-hour B200 rate is the lowest published on-demand price among these five providers. The caveat: Lambda offers no spot tier, so workloads that could tolerate interruption in exchange for lower cost have no path to savings here. Lambda is privately held and working toward an IPO.

...

## What to do about it

1. Identify your primary GPU model requirement (H100, H200, B200, B300, or AMD MI300X/MI355X) before comparing providers, since not all five list all hardware.
2. Check whether you need spot pricing. If yes, Lambda is currently off the table; evaluate CoreWeave, Nebius, or Crusoe instead.
3. Pull the actual published rate cards directly from each provider’s website. List prices change frequently and any third-party comparison (including this one) can lag.
4. If workload reliability matters, weight the SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX 2.0 rating alongside price. CoreWeave’s Platinum score is the only one in this tier.
5. Monitor Groq’s NVIDIA GPU rollout timeline if low-latency inference is your priority workload. The LPU-to-GPU transition could affect service continuity.

The cheapest list price rarely stays cheapest once you factor in spot unavailability, egress, and the engineering cost of a forced migration.

...

Which GPU neocloud has the lowest B200 on-demand price in 2026?

Lambda publishes the lowest on-demand B200 rate among the five major neoclouds at $6.69 per GPU-hour, but it does not offer a spot tier for further savings.
